To choose the right connector of cause: porque (neutral), como (at the start of the sentence), ya que / puesto que (a known cause), dado que, debido a (formal).
To distinguish “gracias a” (positive cause) from “por culpa de” (negative cause).
To express consequence with así que, por eso, por lo tanto, de modo que.
To use “tan + adjective + que” and “tanto/a/os/as + noun + que”.

The end of December. Aunt Viorica has posted on her social network a photo of Ecaterina and Andrés at San Ginés, with their whole story. In three days, the post has been seen by two million people. Ana has come to her house, very angry.
Aunt Viorica, how could you post that photo? I told you not to touch your phone!
As you weren’t answering, I posted it. I sent you three messages to ask your permission.
Because I was on a plane! And besides, it wasn’t me you had to ask, it was Ecaterina.
Since we’re being honest: the story was so beautiful that I couldn’t keep it to myself.
Well, now half the world knows it. A Spanish journalist shared it, so even Madrid television has called Marta.
And is that bad? Thanks to me, Marta’s novel is selling like hot cakes.
(coming in) Good afternoon. I’ve come because Ana asked me to. And because I wanted to tell you something, Viorica.
Ecaterina… I’m so sorry. I didn’t think about the consequences.
Nobody asked my permission; hence at first I was very angry. So many journalists called me that I had to unplug the phone.
Now I’ve read the comments. There are thousands of people who have started looking for someone again because of this story. Or thanks to it. So, Viorica, I forgive you.
(with tears in her eyes) Really? Then… can I do a live stream with you?
“por culpa de” = because of, through the fault of
«Como no contestabas, …»: after the “como” clause there is a clear pause with a rising tone, then the consequence.
Run together: [dea-Í-que]. The stress falls on “ahí”.
bi-RAL: the “v” is pronounced like a soft “b”, and the stress is on the last syllable.
No contesté porque estaba en un avión.
ALWAYS at the start of the sentence
Dado que la autora no ha dado permiso…
Debido al éxito, se reeditará la novela.
Gracias a ti, la novela se vende.
Por culpa del vídeo, tuvo que apagar el móvil.
Causal “como” never comes after the main clause: «Lo publiqué como no contestabas» ✗ → «Como no contestabas, lo publiqué» ✓ or «Lo publiqué porque no contestabas» ✓.
A journalist shared it, so it went viral. (informal and everyday)
She hadn’t given her consent; that’s why she got angry.
Demand has increased. Therefore, the publisher will reprint the book. (formal)
She unplugged the phone, so nobody could reach her.
“De modo que / de manera que” + INDICATIVE = consequence (“so”). + SUBJUNCTIVE = purpose (“so that”): «Habla despacio, de modo que te entiendan» (Speak slowly so that they understand you).
La historia era tan bonita que no podía guardarla.
Me llamaron tantos periodistas que desconecté el teléfono.
Lloró tanto que se le hincharon los ojos.
Don’t mix them up: “tan” before adjectives and adverbs, “tanto” before nouns (and it agrees!) or after verbs. «Tan gente» ✗ → «Tanta gente» ✓.
“De ahí que” presents a consequence as already known or obvious. It takes the SUBJUNCTIVE, even though it expresses a real fact — it’s an exception you have to learn by heart:
Nobody asked her permission; hence she got angry.
She is very demanding; hence her students always pass.
A simpler equivalent with the indicative: «por eso se enfadó». At B2 it’s good to know both; “de ahí que” makes a text more elegant.
Como llovía, nos quedamos en casa.
Nos quedamos en casa como llovía.
Como llovía que nos quedamos en casa.
“There were so many people that we didn’t fit.”
Había tanta gente que no cabíamos.
Había tan gente que no cabíamos.
Había tanto gente que no cabíamos.

A press report in a formal register. Notice the connectors of cause and consequence.
The Madrid publisher that brought out Marta Gil’s first novel in October has announced a second edition, owing to the huge increase in sales over the last two weeks.

The phenomenon began thanks to a post on a social network in which a retired Romanian lady told the true story that inspired the book. Since the post was shared by several journalists, within a few days it had reached several million views.
As the first edition sold out in a week, many bookshops have had to set up waiting lists. Consequently, the publisher has decided to bring the second edition forward to January.
The author has preferred not to give interviews since, as she has explained, her grandfather needs peace and quiet. Hence all media requests are being handled through the publisher.
¿Por qué ha anunciado la editorial una segunda edición?
Debido al aumento de las ventas
¿En cuánto tiempo se agotó la primera edición?
¿Por qué no concede entrevistas la autora?

It all started with a photo. Ana had taken it at San Ginés: Andrés in his wheelchair, his blanket stained with chocolate, laughing; and beside him Ecaterina, with a churro in her hand, looking at him the way you look at someone who has just come back from a very long journey. Ana had sent it to Costel, like all the others. Costel, moved, had forwarded it to Aunt Viorica, because she had asked him to “keep her informed”.

As Ana was on the plane home and wasn’t answering, Viorica decided that silence was a form of permission. That same night she posted the photo on her social network, with a long text written in Romanian and translated into Spanish by Andrei, who had fallen into the trap too. It was called: “Forty years later, love is not forgotten”.

At first nothing special happened. The post got the usual one or two thousand “likes” from her followers, almost all of them Romanian pensioners who thanked her for her recipe videos and her tips on using a phone. But the next morning, a very well-known Spanish journalist, who had a radio show and a million followers, saw it by chance. She found it so beautiful that she shared it with a single comment: “This is the most beautiful thing I’ve read this year.”

From then on, everything happened very fast. Within twenty-four hours, the photo had been seen by half a million people. Within three days, by two million. Spanish, Romanian and even Argentine newspapers wrote articles about “the translator and the bookseller”. Someone discovered that the story appeared in Marta Gil’s novel, so people started looking for the book in bookshops. The first edition sold out in a week.

For Ecaterina, on the other hand, those days were a nightmare. As her name appeared in the post, the journalists found her straight away. They called her at home at all hours. A Romanian television channel turned up outside her building with a camera and a microphone. Ecaterina, who for eighty years had defended her private life tooth and nail, unplugged the phone, closed the shutters and didn’t leave the house for two days.

In Madrid, the situation was even worse. Owing to the novel’s sudden fame, several journalists tried to get into the flat on the calle del Prado. One even rang the bell pretending to be the postman. Marta, very worried about her grandfather, had to ask the neighbours for help, and they organised shifts to watch the front door. Luckily, Andrés knew nothing about it, as in those days he was hardly ever awake.

Costel was the first to apologise. He called Ana from a car park near Bratislava, with the voice of a child who has broken a vase. He explained that he had forwarded the photo because Viorica had sworn she only wanted to show it to her friends from church. “I trusted her because she’s older,” he said. “And because she promised me a cake.” Ana couldn’t help laughing, although she was still angry.

At home, meanwhile, Rosa Elena had become a little celebrity. As one of Viorica’s photos showed her drawing of the book tree, which Ecaterina had taken to Andrés, the nursery teacher had seen it online and hung it on the classroom wall. Rosa Elena explained to all her classmates that the gentleman in Madrid was Señora Ecaterina’s boyfriend, and that she had helped them find each other. Mihai decided not to correct her.

Ana was so angry that she couldn’t sleep all night. The next day she went to Aunt Viorica’s ready to give her a piece of her mind. She found her sitting on the sofa, phone in hand and eyes full of tears, reading the comments. There were a hundred thousand of them. Viorica didn’t defend herself. She just said to Ana: “Read this.” And she handed her the phone.

Ana read. There was a comment from a man in Valparaíso who said that, thanks to the story, he had called his brother, whom he hadn’t spoken to for twenty years. A woman from Cluj wrote that she had looked up her first boyfriend online, who lived in Canada, and that he had answered in less than an hour. A boy from Seville said he was going to write to his grandmother that very night, because he hadn’t called her for months.

There were hundreds of stories like that. People who had left without saying goodbye. Letters that had never been sent. Friends who had drifted apart because of a silly argument. And they all said the same thing, in different words and in different languages: that Ecaterina and Andrés’s story had given them the courage to do something they hadn’t dared to do for years.

Ana sat for a long time with the phone in her hand. She still thought Viorica had no right to post the photo without permission. But she was no longer sure it had been only a mistake. She called Ecaterina and told her there was something she had to see. Ecaterina refused at first. Ana insisted. In the end Ecaterina agreed, although she made it clear she was only coming because Ana asked her to, not for Viorica.

She arrived an hour later, with her coat, her stick and her most serious face, the one she put on when a student mixed up “ser” and “estar” for the tenth time. She sat down on a chair, away from Viorica, and put on her glasses. Ana handed her the phone. Ecaterina read in silence for half an hour. Nobody said anything. Viorica wrung her hands on the sofa. Ana made tea for the three of them, although nobody touched it.

At last, Ecaterina took off her glasses. She said nobody had asked her permission and that, therefore, she had every right to be angry. Viorica lowered her head. But then Ecaterina added that she had spent forty years without daring to do what thousands of strangers had just done in a week, and that this, in a way, was also a little thanks to her. Hence, although it was hard for her, she had decided to forgive her.

Viorica burst into tears of relief. She stood up to hug her, but Ecaterina stopped her with a gesture. She told her she forgave her on one condition: that she never again posted anything about her, Andrés or Marta without asking first. Viorica swore it on all her followers. Then, with the excitement of a little girl, she asked if she could do a live stream with her. Ecaterina told her not to push it.

The next day Pilar, Andrés’s daughter, called her too, from Seville. It was the first time they had spoken. Pilar told her that as a little girl she had secretly hated that foreign woman who spent her nights in the back room with her father, because she was afraid she would take him away from her. And that now, forty years later, she wanted to thank her, because since her return her father smiled in a way she hadn’t seen him smile since she was a child.

That same afternoon, Marta called Ecaterina. She told her she had read some of the comments aloud to her grandfather, during one of his few moments of lucidity. Andrés had listened with his eyes closed. When she had finished, he had asked her whether all those people had started looking for someone again because of the two of them. Marta had told him yes. And he, after thinking about it for a while, had remarked: “Then the bookshop hasn’t closed.”

But the story wasn’t over yet. A week later, at the beginning of January, Ecaterina received two emails on the same day. The first was from the publisher in Bucharest. Owing to the novel’s success in Spain, they wanted to bring out the Romanian translation much earlier than planned, in the spring, and asked whether she could finish it in time. Ecaterina, who had already translated twelve of the twenty chapters, said yes without thinking twice.

The second email was from the Madrid Book Fair. They were inviting her to present the Romanian translation together with Marta, at the end of May, in the Retiro park. At the end of the message there was a sentence added by the fair’s director: “If Señor Andrés Gil can come with you, we will keep a seat for him in the front row, by the brightest window of the marquee.”

Ecaterina read the two emails three times. Then she called Marta. She asked how her grandfather was. Marta answered that he was weaker, but that every morning he asked whether a letter had come from Bucharest. Ecaterina told her about the fair. At the other end of the line there was a long silence. Then Marta said, her voice shaking, that she didn’t know whether her grandfather would make it to May. But that if he did, he wouldn’t miss it for anything in the world.

That night Ecaterina didn’t switch on the television or look at her phone. She sat in the kitchen, with Rayuela and Marta’s novel open on the table, and translated until three in the morning. As she could no longer see well at night, she used a huge magnifying glass Mihai had given her for Christmas. She translated four pages. They seemed to her the four best pages she had ever translated.

Before going to bed, she wrote a message to Ana. It was the first message she had written without a single spelling mistake, although she later confessed that Andrei had installed a spell checker for her. It read: “Dear Ana: you were right. Silence hurts too, only more slowly. That’s why I’ve decided not to keep quiet any more. In May we’re going to Madrid. Tell Costel: we’ll keep him a seat in the front row.”
